sourceIssues.locator: Corollary 3.2, p.951, as applied in §11, p.971, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 189 (2019), 945–978 (public copy of the published PDF at bimsa.net, SHA-256 1eab0797…a0ab)
sourceIssues.printed: "Corollary 3.2. Let A ⊂ Ω × X be a closed, constructible complex analytic set that is Γ × {id}-invariant, and such that A ∩ (F × X) is definable. Then (q × id)(A) ⊂ X × X is a constructible algebraic subset. Proof. It follows from Corollary 2.3 as above." In §11: "Let V′_{n,ℓ} be the image of G(C) × id_ℓ(Ω̂) restricted to J^n_ℓ Ω, and V_{n,ℓ} its constructible algebraic (by Corollary 3.2) image in J^n_ℓ X", and likewise "an integrable algebraic (by Corollary 3.2) foliation".
sourceIssues.correction: State and prove the version actually used. For a definable, Γ-invariant, constructible (not necessarily closed) analytic set A in the relevant jet space, its image under the uniformization is constructible algebraic. The proof needs that this image is again a definable constructible analytic set, for example via a finite stratification of A into locally closed analytic pieces whose images are analytic, before Corollary 2.3 applies.
sourceIssues.reason: As printed, the hypothesis "closed, constructible" makes the corollary a restatement of Theorem 3.1. It does not cover its uses in §11, where V′_{n,ℓ} and W′_{n,ℓ} are images of algebraic maps, constructible but not shown to be closed. Those uses are also in jet spaces J_ℓΩ → J_ℓX rather than in Ω × X. The one-line proof gives no reason why the image of a non-closed constructible analytic set is constructible analytic. Noted by the extraction (item quotient-constructible-algebraic).

sourceIssues.locator: Corollary 9.3 and its proof, p.965, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 189 (2019), 945–978 (public copy of the published PDF at bimsa.net, SHA-256 1eab0797…a0ab)
sourceIssues.printed: "Let {φ_1, …, φ_N} be a C-basis of modular functions." Proof: "… it follows that tr.deg_C C({z_i}, {φ_j^{(ν)}}) = dim G + n. The algebraic independence will therefore follow as soon as we show that the transcendence degree of C(z_1, …, z_n) is equal to dim G."
sourceIssues.correction: "Let φ_1, …, φ_N generate the field of modular functions", and in the proof: "… as soon as we show that the transcendence degree over C of the field generated by the φ_j and their partial derivatives up to order k is equal to dim G."
sourceIssues.reason: C(z_1, …, z_n) has transcendence degree n. The proof then shows that the Zariski closure W of the projection has dimension dim G, which concerns the field generated by the φ_j^{(ν)}. The field of modular functions is not a finite-dimensional C-vector space; finitely many generators of it are meant. Noted by the extraction (item modular-derivative-trdeg).

sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Lemma 11.1, p.969, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 189 (2019), 945–978 (public copy of the published PDF at bimsa.net, SHA-256 1eab0797…a0ab)
sourceIssues.printed: "We partition X_{d,d} into subsets X^i_{d,d} consisting of all pairs (φ, ψ) satisfying Stab φ_i = Stab φ_{i+1}, where φ_i denotes φ up to the i-th order, and i is the smallest such integer. Note that this is indeed a partition since each time Stab φ_i ≠ Stab φ_{i+1} the dimension of Stab φ_{i+1} is at least 1 smaller than that of Stab φ_i."
sourceIssues.correction: A strict inclusion Stab φ_{i+1} ⊊ Stab φ_i of algebraic subgroups need not lower the dimension. So the choice m = d = dim G, and the claim that the X^i_{d,d} cover X_{d,d}, need a further argument that bounds the number of dimension-preserving drops uniformly, for example through the component groups or via Scanlon's finite-order orbit results.
sourceIssues.reason: A proper closed subgroup of the same dimension is a union of fewer connected components of the same identity component. Along the chain of stabilizers, such drops can occur without any drop in dimension, and the argument counts only dimension drops. The lemma asserts only that some m = m(G, q, k) exists; the proof's value m = d is not established. Noted by the extraction (the report's check 4).

sourceIssues.locator: Theorem 11.3 and its proof, p.971, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 189 (2019), 945–978 (public copy of the published PDF at bimsa.net, SHA-256 1eab0797…a0ab)
sourceIssues.printed: "Theorem 11.3. Let k be a positive integer, r ≥ 2, and m as above. Consider a map (w, u, v) : Δ^k → Ω̂ × X × J^n_r X. If the image of (w, u, v) lands in V_{k,m} × V_{n,r} and the image of Tv lands in W_{n,r}, and if v restricts to u, then there exists g ∈ G(C) such that (w, u, v) = L(w, g, r)." Proof: "… Thus we may write g(t) = gn(t) for a function n(t) ∈ N. However, since v restricts to u, it follows that n(t) is the identity function."
sourceIssues.correction: "v restricts to u" is not defined, and read as the zeroth-order condition used in the proof, namely that the value of v is u, the theorem is false. A first-order compatibility must be added: du equals the first-order part of v applied to dw, as holds for every L(w, g, r), or the full chain-rule compatibility of the jet v along w with the jets of u. The proof's last step must use it.
sourceIssues.reason:
Work locally on a modular curve (n = k = 1) with Γ torsion-free, near a point where q′ ≠ 0. Put w(t) = 2t, u(t) = q(t) and v(t) = J_r q(id_r(t)). Then:
- The m-jets of u are those of q ∘ (z ↦ z/2) ∘ w, so they lie in V_{k,m}.
- v lies in V_{n,r}, and Tv lies in W_{n,r}, since v moves along the leaf through the identity.
- The value of v at t is q(t) = u(t).
By Theorem 11.2, any g with u = q ∘ g ∘ w is z ↦ γ(z/2) with γ ∈ Γ. For such g, J_r(q ∘ g) at w(t) = 2t has first derivative q′(t)/2, while v has q′(t), so (w, u, v) ≠ L(w, g, r) for every g. In the proof, the leaf decomposition of v gives g(t) = τ_{−t}, the translation, with trivial leaf constant and n(t) = τ_{−t} ≠ id, although the zeroth-order condition holds. Every L(w, g, r) satisfies du = v_1 dw, which fails here (q′ ≠ 2q′). The same wording is in arXiv v3. The Ax–Schanuel theorems themselves are not claimed to fail. Noted by the extraction (item triple-characterization-obligation), which gave this example.

sourceIssues.locator: §12.4, direct proof of Theorem 9.1 from Theorem 12.1, pp.974–975, in the published version, Annals of Mathematics 189 (2019), 945–978 (public copy of the published PDF at bimsa.net, SHA-256 1eab0797…a0ab)
sourceIssues.printed: "On the other hand, since r has full rank, by our non-degeneracy assumption we may find a map φ : Ω → Δ^k such that (z, r, s, ...) ∘ φ is the identity, and thus the two fields are equal." and "(z, x, y) is a uniformized locus of rank k = rank(z) = dim U."
sourceIssues.correction: Obtain the field equality C(z, r, s, …; x, R, S, …) = C(z, r, s, …; x, q_i^{(ν)} ∘ z) by linear algebra. The matrix r(t) is invertible, so ∂q_i/∂z_p(z(t)) = Σ_j R^i_j(t)(r(t)^{−1})^j_p, and the higher derivatives of q at z(t) are recovered recursively from S, s, r, and so on. Do not identify rank(z) with dim U; the final dimension count uses dim(z).
sourceIssues.reason: Along a k-dimensional locus U of non-degenerate jets, the base point z(t) can be constant, or of rank less than n, while the formal first-order coordinates r(t) vary. So no φ with z ∘ φ = id need exist, and rank(z) can be smaller than dim U. Full rank of the formal matrix r is what makes the linear recovery work. The concluding inequality dim Zcl(A, B) − dim Zcl(A) ≥ dim(A, B) − dim A only needs dim(z). §12.4 is a second proof of Theorem 9.1, which is proved directly in §10, so no result depends on it. Checked on the page image. Noted by the extraction (the report's check 6).
